extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism students, and media critics interested in standards for investigative reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for producing rigorous investigative journalism, with emphasis on verification, corroboration, editorial oversight, and the resources and practices that prevent major reporting failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic reporting, editing, and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting, editing, and fact-checking must follow basic, avoidable standards; failures in these areas led to the Rolling Stone UVA story collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Columbia report found “a host of basic reporting, editing, and fact-checking failures and wrong turns that were avoidable.” Editorial and fact-checking steps should catch clear problems before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration of first-person accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts told entirely from a single narrator must be corroborated by independent sources before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UVA story relied on Jackie’s recollection; the magazine ‘opted not to interview people who could corroborate Jackie’s story’ (though reporters had sought some friends and then gave up). Interview potential corroborators rather than relying on a single account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify with documents and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documentary evidence—legal documents, badges, paychecks, permit files—to verify claims in investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Times reporters reviewed legal documents, work badges, and paychecks; the Wall Street Journal team poured over permit files to build a database. Documentary verification strengthens claims and supports publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing unverifiable accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Unverifiable or unreliable narratives should be caught and cut before publication; publishing them damages credibility and can have real-world harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that ‘unreliable or outright false narratives like Jackie’s, when discovered, are caught early, before publication, and are cut.’ If unverifiable accounts are published, the result can be retractions, libel suits, and harm to public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce 'bulletproofed', thoroughly fact-checked accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative pieces should be 'bulletproofed' through extensive fact-checking to minimize errors and avoid retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites many recent investigative examples that were extensively verified; the absence of such rigorous checking contributed to the Rolling Stone failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site reporting and firsthand observation
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, reporters should do in-person reporting and direct observation as part of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a reporter ‘drove to factories, spoke to underage workers as they left’ and journalists accompanied divers to examine underwater cables—firsthand work bolsters credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of data, coding, and databases for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ technical tools—code, databases, data collection—to analyze records and uncover corroborating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WSJ example: collecting data from thousands of permit files and building a database; technical approaches can reveal patterns and evidence not apparent from interviews alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named on-the-record sources strengthen stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Having named, on-the-record sources—even a single credible named source—makes a story stronger and more defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ProPublica/New York story: ‘Just one doctor would speak on the record. But the story is stronger for having that one named former colleague.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and exhaustive sourcing effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting requires persistent outreach—cold calls, emails, repeated attempts—to find sources and corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes ‘an untold number of hours of cold calls, emails, and rejections’ that lead to finding sources; reporters must endure rejections to secure testimony and documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and overcome institutional resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should expect institutions (universities, corporations, agencies) to refuse or obfuscate and plan strategies to obtain information despite that resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Columbia (the university) ‘didn’t make it easy on the journalists… refusing to make any of its leaders available’ yet reporters pursued alternative sources and documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight: editors must be discerning and demand verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should rigorously question reporters, require corroboration, and not accept unverifiable narratives in the name of protecting sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenner’s defense that editors were trying to protect a victim is contrasted with the Columbia report’s finding that editorial decisions (e.g., stopping efforts to interview corroborators) were mistakes; editors must push for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance victim protection with verification needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Protecting the identity and dignity of vulnerable sources is important, but not at the expense of necessary corroboration that determines accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenner claimed the magazine avoided interviewing others 'to avoid further identifying and victimizing [her]'; the Columbia report found that more effort at corroboration should have been pursued even while protecting victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardrails against fabrication and incentive problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms must maintain guardrails (culture, processes, oversight) to prevent reporters from fabricating stories or cutting corners due to fame-seeking or competitive pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Janet Cooke, Stephen Glass, Jayson Blair) show fabrication occurs when guardrails are weak; competitive incentives and lack of oversight can encourage misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest resources and time appropriate to investigative complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative work is expensive, laborious, and complex; adequate staffing, time, and funding are required to do it properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes shrinking budgets, low morale, and turnover can cause good stories to go untold or collapse; fund investigative projects sufficiently to allow thorough verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent audit and accountability after failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When major reporting failures occur, independent audits and transparent reviews help identify mistakes and restore accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenner asked Columbia Journalism School to produce an independent audit; the Columbia report identified failings rather than exonerating the magazine—showing the value of independent review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from corrections and minimize retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat corrections as part of the process, but strive to minimize retractions through rigorous pre-publication verification and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts 'errors and corrections' (common) with 'vanishingly few retractions' in mainstream investigative journalism, framing retractions as a failure of pre-publication processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership accountability and candid acknowledgment of errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership should acknowledge failures candidly and avoid deflecting blame in order to preserve institutional credibility and learn from mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenner's attempts to frame Rolling Stone as a victim are criticized; honest leadership acknowledgment supports accountability and corrective action.
